content: The documents referenced outline critical interventions required to address pneumonia and diarrhea effectively. Many countries have already begun implementing these strategies, recognizing that these two diseases are best managed through a coordinated approach. Pneumonia and diarrhea share common determinants, control strategies, and delivery systems. Both are caused by multiple pathogens, meaning no single intervention can address them entirely. For instance, Zambia has established a Child Health Technical Working Group that addresses pneumonia and diarrhea alongside other health issues. In many countries, controlling these diseases forms the foundation of primary healthcare (PHC). Addressing their prevention and management as integrated packages strengthens weak health systems. The Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Pneumonia and Diarrhea (GAPPD) provides a comprehensive framework of key interventions to protect, prevent, and treat these diseases in children under five years of age. It also suggests supporting activities to enhance and accelerate the implementation of proven interventions. The GAPPD does not propose a change in direction but identifies opportunities to better integrate activities, capture synergies, and improve efficiency. It offers an integrated framework of interventions to control pneumonia and diarrhea and outlines supporting activities to improve and expedite their implementation. The GAPPD is primarily intended for national governments and their partners, as well as global organizations, donor agencies, and other stakeholders working on pneumonia and diarrhea. It also emphasizes the critical role of community-level groups and individuals in effectively implementing the strategy. The GAPPD builds on and strengthens existing initiatives aimed at improving child health, such as the Global Strategy for Women’s and Children’s Health, the United Nations Commission on Life-Saving Commodities for Women and Children, and the Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP). These initiatives focus on improving financing, strengthening policies, and enhancing service delivery to reduce child mortality from pneumonia and diarrhea. The GAPPD envisions interventions for controlling pneumonia and diarrhea in children under five through three key strategies: protecting children by promoting good health practices, preventing illness through immunization and healthy environments, and treating sick children with appropriate care. Proven interventions include exclusive breastfeeding for six months, adequate complementary feeding, vitamin A supplementation, vaccines (e.g., for pertussis, measles, Hib, PCV, and rotavirus), handwashing with soap, safe drinking water, improved sanitation, and reducing household air pollution. Treatment strategies include improved care-seeking behavior, case management at health facilities and community levels, and the use of essential supplies like oral rehydration salts (ORS), zinc, antibiotics, and oxygen. These interventions have demonstrated significant reductions in child mortality and morbidity when implemented effectively and consistently. Despite the availability of these interventions, coverage remains insufficient to achieve the desired impact. For example, only 37% of infants under six months are exclusively breastfed, and just 33% of children with diarrhea receive ORS and continued feeding. Improved sanitation facilities are available in only 40% of homes, and 76% have access to improved drinking water sources. Addressing these gaps requires better coordination, increased resources, and stronger health systems. The GAPPD emphasizes equity in access to interventions, prioritizing disadvantaged populations at the highest risk of death and severe illness. Strategies to improve coverage include expanding the roles of community health workers (CHWs), reducing financial barriers, increasing human resources, and engaging the private sector. Additionally, the GAPPD highlights the importance of addressing pneumonia and diarrhea in humanitarian emergencies, where these diseases are leading causes of death in children under five. Vaccination, safe drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene are immediate priorities in such settings. Urbanization poses unique challenges, as many children in urban areas live in overcrowded and unhygienic conditions that facilitate disease transmission. While urban areas often have better access to health facilities, many children lack even basic services.
